metadata.description: 85 ecological relationships between 29 UK & Ireland wildlife species

relationshipTypes.intraguild_predation: Species compete AND one predates the other
relationshipTypes.disease_vector: Species A transmits disease harmful to Species B
relationshipTypes.seed_dispersal: Species A disperses seeds/propagules of Species B
relationshipTypes.habitat_provider: Species A provides critical habitat for Species B
relationshipTypes.soil_engineering: Species A engineers soil benefiting Species B
relationshipTypes.nutrient_cycling: Species A delivers nutrients benefiting Species B
relationshipTypes.indirect_positive: Species A indirectly benefits Species B via intermediate effects
relationshipTypes.herbivory: Species A feeds on plant Species B

relationships.description: Otters predate salmon; salmonids are a major dietary component, especially in Scottish rivers.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Otter diet shifts to alternative prey (crayfish, frogs) when salmon decline.
relationships.source_citation: Carss, Kruuk & Conroy (1990) Journal of Fish Biology 37:935–944

relationships.description: Otters predate native crayfish in remaining populations.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Loss of native crayfish shifts otter predation to other freshwater species.
relationships.source_citation: Britton et al. (2017) Knowledge & Management of Aquatic Ecosystems 418:12

relationships.description: Otters consume frogs, especially in spring breeding aggregations. Frog bones frequently found in otter spraints.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Frog decline reduces a supplementary food source for otters.
relationships.source_citation: Mammal Society otter profile; Wildlife Online

relationships.description: Native predator of water voles, but unlike mink, otters cannot enter vole burrows. Voles evolved to coexist with otter predation.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Unlike mink predation, otter predation is sustainable and does not drive vole decline.
relationships.source_citation: Wildlife Trusts; IUCN UK Peatland Programme

relationships.description: Sand eels dominate grey seal diet in multiple UK regions.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Sand eel decline forces seals to switch to gadid fish, buffering their population but increasing pressure on commercial fisheries.

relationships.description: Seals opportunistically take salmon near estuaries and river mouths.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Seal predation adds additional pressure to already declining salmon stocks.
relationships.source_citation: Sea Mammal Research Unit diet studies

relationships.description: Sand eels are the primary food for puffin chicks. Puffin decline is directly linked to sand eel loss.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Sand eel decline causes puffin chick starvation and breeding failure across North Sea colonies.
relationships.source_citation: RSPB Revive Our Seas (2021); Seabirds Count (JNCC, 2023)

relationships.description: Salmon feed on sand eels during their marine phase.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Sand eel decline reduces salmon condition and survival at sea.
relationships.source_citation: Hendry & Cragg-Hine (2003) Conserving Natura 2000 Rivers No. 7

relationships.description: Primary driver of 94% water vole decline. Female mink enter burrows and kill mothers with pups.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Water vole extinction from river reaches simplifies riparian habitat, reducing invertebrate and amphibian diversity.
relationships.source_citation: Rushton et al. (2000) Journal of Applied Ecology 37:475–490

relationships.description: Mink predate kingfishers and other bank-nesting birds along waterways.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Mink presence suppresses kingfisher nesting success along affected rivers.
relationships.source_citation: ZSL Water Vole programme; Suffolk Wildlife Trust

relationships.description: Mink predate amphibians including frogs along waterways.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Mink predation adds pressure to rural frog populations already stressed by habitat loss.

relationships.description: Kingfishers take tadpoles and small froglets from shallow water.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Frog decline reduces food diversity for kingfishers, increasing dependence on fish.

relationships.description: Amphibians feature as supplementary prey for tawny owls.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Frog decline narrows tawny owl diet breadth.

relationships.description: Earthworms consumed by tawny owls, particularly during wet weather.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline reduces alternative prey when primary prey (voles) are scarce.

relationships.description: Red squirrels documented as occasional prey in owl pellet analyses.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Red squirrel decline removes a prey option from tawny owl diet.
relationships.source_citation: Cramp (1985) Birds of the Western Palearctic Vol. 4

relationships.description: Jays appear in owl pellet analyses as occasional prey.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Minimal population-level effect; illustrates woodland predator-prey complexity.
relationships.source_citation: Glue (1972) BTO Avian Predator Food Survey

relationships.description: Frogs occasionally taken; voles are primary prey.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Frog availability provides dietary buffering during vole population crashes.
relationships.source_citation: Barn Owl Trust; Natural History Museum

relationships.description: Minor dietary component in adverse conditions.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline reduces fallback food during prey scarcity.
relationships.source_citation: Barn Owl Trust; Somerset Wildlife Trust

relationships.description: Harriers prey on grouse chicks during breeding season; can reduce grouse numbers below shooting viability.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Triggers illegal persecution of harriers by gamekeepers, suppressing harrier population to fraction of capacity.
relationships.source_citation: Thirgood & Redpath (2008) Journal of Applied Ecology 45:982–991

relationships.description: Occasional predation; hedgehog spines usually deter foxes. Some scavenging of roadkill.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Fox predation is minor compared to badger intraguild effects and habitat loss.
relationships.source_citation: Morris, The New Hedgehog Book; Wildlife Online

relationships.description: Frogs are a documented component of fox diet.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Fox predation contributes to cumulative predation pressure on rural frogs.

relationships.description: Grey squirrels found in urban fox diet studies.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Foxes provide some natural control on grey squirrel populations in urban areas.

relationships.description: Significant dietary component; earthworms can provide up to 60% of caloric intake.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline forces foxes to increase predation on other species.

relationships.description: Major grouse predator; fox control is central to grouse moor management.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Fox control for grouse also benefits ground-nesting skylarks in adjacent farmland.
relationships.source_citation: Hudson & Newborn (1995) Manual of Red Grouse, Game Conservancy Trust

relationships.description: Foxes prey on ground-nesting skylarks and their eggs.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Fox predation is one of multiple pressures on declining skylark populations.

relationships.description: Squirrels form part of varied mammalian prey.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Minor additional predation pressure on already declining red squirrel populations.

relationships.description: Earthworms constitute ~80% of badger diet. Hundreds consumed per night.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline is a bottom-up pressure on badger populations; forces dietary shifts.
relationships.source_citation: Neal & Cheeseman (1996) Badgers, Poyser; Woodland Trust

relationships.description: Documented predator of common frogs.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Badger population increase adds predation pressure on rural frog populations.

relationships.description: Major dietary component alongside beetles and slugs.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline reduces hedgehog food availability, compounding habitat and badger pressures.

relationships.description: Occasional predation documented.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Hedgehog decline reduces one predation pressure on frog populations.

relationships.description: Worms are important invertebrate prey for skylarks.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline in farmland reduces food availability during chick-rearing.

relationships.description: Frogs actively prey on earthworms in terrestrial habitats.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline reduces frog food in terrestrial phase.

relationships.description: Only UK predator that can overcome hedgehog spines. Both compete for invertebrates. Experimental badger removal doubled hedgehog counts.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Rising badger populations contribute to hedgehog decline through both predation and competition for invertebrate prey.
relationships.source_citation: Trewby et al. (2014) PLOS ONE 9(4):e95477; Doncaster (1992) Proc. R. Soc. B 249:113–117

relationships.description: Exploitative competition for food, especially acorns. Greys digest tannins more efficiently, depleting food before reds can access it.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Red squirrels excluded from deciduous woodland; confined to conifer refugia in Scotland and northern England.
relationships.source_citation: Gurnell et al. (2004) Journal of Animal Ecology 73:26–35; Kenward & Holm (1993)

relationships.description: Competition for invertebrate food; one badger consumes ~5× more invertebrates than one hedgehog.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Food competition forces hedgehogs into urban gardens where badger density is lower.

relationships.description: Otter recovery displaces mink. Mink occupancy dropped from 77% to 23% within one year of otter arrival in Upper Thames.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Mink displacement triggers positive cascade: water vole recovery, reduced predation on kingfishers and amphibians.
relationships.source_citation: Bonesi & Macdonald (2004) Oikos 106:9–18; McDonald et al. (2007) Diversity & Distributions 13:92–98

relationships.description: Invasive signal crayfish (displacing native crayfish) predate salmonid eggs and compete with juvenile salmon for refuges.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Signal crayfish invasion simultaneously threatens native crayfish and adds pressure on salmon reproduction.

relationships.description: Greys carry squirrelpox virus (SQPV) asymptomatically; ~100% fatal to reds. Accelerates replacement ~20× faster than competition alone.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Disease front moves northward through Scotland; reds can only survive where greys are excluded.
relationships.source_citation: Tompkins et al. (2002) Proc. R. Soc. B 269:529–533; Rushton et al. (2006)

relationships.description: Primary long-distance dispersal agent of oak acorns. Responsible for post-Ice Age northward expansion of oaks. A single jay caches up to 5,000 acorns per autumn.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Jay decline would dramatically slow oak regeneration, threatening the 2,300+ species that depend on oak.
relationships.source_citation: Bossema (1979) Behaviour 70:1–116; den Ouden et al. (2005)

relationships.description: Red squirrels cache and eat acorns; unforgotten caches germinate into new trees.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Red squirrel decline reduces one seed dispersal pathway for oaks.
relationships.source_citation: Kenward & Holm (1993) Proc. R. Soc. B 251:187–194

relationships.description: Grey squirrels cache acorns but also exploit crops before ripening due to superior tannin tolerance.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Greys consume more acorns before caching, reducing regeneration potential compared to red squirrel dispersal.

relationships.description: Major pollinator of heather. Heather nectar contains compounds that protect bumblebees from gut parasite Crithidia bombi.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Heather moorland loss removes a medicinal food source, increasing bumblebee disease susceptibility.
relationships.source_citation: Koch et al., Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, Current Biology

relationships.description: Pollinates hawthorn blossom. Hawthorn provides key early-season nectar source for emerging queens.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Hawthorn removal from hedgerows reduces critical early spring food for queen bumblebees.
relationships.source_citation: Woodland Trust; Jacobs (2008) PhD thesis, Stirling University

relationships.description: Important early spring nectar source in woodland for bumblebees emerging from hibernation.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Bluebell decline would remove a critical early-season food source.

relationships.description: Adults nectar on heather flowers, particularly in upland habitats.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Heather loss reduces foraging habitat for already-declining tortoiseshell populations.
relationships.source_citation: Butterfly Conservation UK; Scottish Wildlife Trust

relationships.description: Adults visit hawthorn blossom and hedgerow flowers for nectar.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Hedgerow loss reduces nectar availability across flight corridors.

relationships.description: Provides critical nesting cavities in natural tree holes. Tawny owls depend on mature trees.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Loss of mature oaks forces tawny owls into nest boxes or suboptimal sites, reducing breeding success.

relationships.description: Provides nesting habitat and primary food source (acorns).
relationships.cascadeEffect: Oak decline would reduce jay populations, further slowing oak regeneration in a negative feedback loop.

relationships.description: Provides habitat, nesting sites (dreys), and food in mixed woodland.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Loss of mature oak woodland shrinks red squirrel habitat in remaining strongholds.

relationships.description: Optimal habitat; grey squirrel density correlates positively with oak canopy coverage.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Oak-dominated woodland supports highest grey squirrel densities.
relationships.source_citation: Gurnell et al. (2004) Journal of Animal Ecology

relationships.description: Woodland habitat for setts; oak leaf litter supports the earthworm populations badgers depend on.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Oak woodland loss reduces both shelter and food base for badgers.

relationships.description: Deciduous canopy allows the brief spring light window that bluebells need to flower.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Change in canopy species (e.g., to evergreen conifers) eliminates bluebell populations.

relationships.description: Historical nest cavities in old oaks; some still used alongside modern nest boxes.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Loss of ancient oaks reduces natural nesting sites.

relationships.description: Dense thorny hedgerows provide shelter, nesting, and hibernation habitat. Hedgerows also serve as movement corridors.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Hedgerow removal isolates hedgehog populations and removes hibernation sites.

relationships.description: Hedgerows structure farmland landscape. Invertebrates in hedgerow base provide food.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Hedgerow loss simplifies farmland, reducing invertebrate food availability for skylarks.

relationships.description: Haws eaten by jays in autumn/winter; hedgerow provides nesting cover.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Hedgerow loss reduces winter food and nesting options for jays.

relationships.description: Hedgerows provide cover, denning habitat, and movement corridors for foxes.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Hedgerow loss exposes foxes to persecution and reduces hunting cover.

relationships.description: Primary food plant (~90% of diet) and nesting habitat. Red grouse are entirely dependent on heather moorland.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Heather loss directly causes red grouse population collapse in affected areas.
relationships.source_citation: Hudson (1986) Red Grouse, Game Conservancy Trust

relationships.description: Provides nest concealment and prey-base support in moorland habitats.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Heather moorland loss reduces hen harrier breeding habitat.
relationships.source_citation: Redpath et al. (1998); Amar et al. (2008) Biological Conservation

relationships.description: Upland heather provides nectar resource for adult butterflies.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Moorland degradation reduces nectar availability in upland habitats.

relationships.description: Mature trees historically provided nest cavities; now mostly buildings serve this role.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Historical loss of ancient trees was an early driver of swift nest site decline.

relationships.description: Burrowing creates soil structure, improves drainage, and recycles nutrients supporting tree growth.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline degrades soil health beneath oaks, reducing growth rates and resilience to disease.
relationships.source_citation: Darwin (1881); Blouin et al. (2013) European Journal of Soil Science 64:161–182

relationships.description: Improves soil structure and nutrient cycling in woodland. Earthworms increase plant production by an average of 25%.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline in woodland soils reduces nutrient cycling that supports bluebell growth.
relationships.source_citation: Van Groenigen et al. (2014) Scientific Reports 4:6365

relationships.description: Nutrient cycling in moorland soils supports heather growth.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline in moorland soils reduces nutrient availability for heather.
relationships.source_citation: Blouin et al. (2013); Earthworm Society of Britain

relationships.description: Improves soil fertility beneath hedgerows.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline reduces soil quality in hedgerow base, affecting hedgerow health.

relationships.description: Salmon carcasses deliver marine-derived nitrogen and phosphorus to riparian vegetation via spawning and predator dispersal.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Salmon decline reduces nutrient input to riparian ecosystems, impoverishing riverside woodlands.
relationships.source_citation: Sheringham et al. (2022) The Holocene; Bernthal et al. (2022) Aquatic Conservation

relationships.description: Marine-derived nutrients from salmon carcasses boost terrestrial soil invertebrate communities in riparian zones.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Salmon decline reduces nutrient subsidies that support riparian earthworm populations.
relationships.source_citation: Woodward et al. (2021) Frontiers in Ecology & Evolution 9:675261

relationships.description: Water vole burrowing and grazing creates diverse riparian habitat structure benefiting amphibian populations.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Water vole loss leads to vegetation homogenisation, reducing habitat quality for frogs and other amphibians.
relationships.source_citation: Bryce (2006) PhD thesis, University of Aberdeen; Wildlife Trusts

relationships.description: ~90% of adult diet is young heather shoots. Grouse grazing influences heather growth patterns.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Grouse absence reduces grazing pressure, potentially allowing heather to become rank and less productive.
relationships.source_citation: Hudson (1986) Red Grouse, Game Conservancy Trust

relationships.description: Bark stripping causes significant damage to young trees (10–40 years). Can kill trees through ring-barking. £37M annual cost.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Bark stripping threatens the next generation of mature oaks, potentially cascading to all 2,300+ oak-dependent species.

relationships.description: Swifts are aerial insectivores feeding on aphids, flies, and small beetles. They generally avoid stinging insects but share the aerial insect food web.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Aerial insect decline reduces food for both swifts and creates a shared pressure across insectivorous species.

relationships.description: Otter recovery suppresses American mink through competitive displacement, indirectly benefiting water voles — a mesopredator release reversal.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Otter presence enables water vole recovery by removing mink predation pressure.
relationships.source_citation: McDonald et al. (2007) Diversity & Distributions; Bonesi & Macdonald (2004)

relationships.description: Otter recovery displaces mink, reducing predation pressure on bank-nesting kingfishers.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Kingfisher nesting success improves along rivers where otters have displaced mink.

relationships.description: Late-season nectar source when many other flowers have finished. Medicinal nectar reduces parasite load.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Heather loss removes a critical late-season food and medicinal resource for bumblebees.
relationships.source_citation: Koch et al. Current Biology (Kew research)

relationships.description: Oak woodland supports diverse understory flowering plants that feed bumblebees.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Woodland loss reduces foraging habitat diversity for pollinators.

relationships.description: Woodland provides denning sites and hunting habitat for foxes.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Woodland fragmentation reduces fox habitat connectivity.

relationships.description: Woodland ponds and damp areas beneath oaks provide breeding and foraging habitat for frogs.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Loss of woodland ponds reduces frog breeding sites.

relationships.description: Hedgerow margins support vole populations that are the primary prey of barn owls.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Hedgerow loss reduces rough grassland margins where voles thrive, impacting barn owl foraging.

relationships.description: Hedgerow bases provide damp shelter and overwintering habitat for frogs in farmland.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Hedgerow removal exposes frogs to desiccation and predation.

relationships.description: Salmon are major prey for otters; salmon availability influences otter body condition and territory size.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Salmon decline forces otters to diversify diet, increasing pressure on other freshwater prey species.
relationships.source_citation: Carss, Kruuk & Conroy (1990) Journal of Fish Biology 37:935–944

relationships.description: Kingfishers take salmon parr and fry from shallow riffles.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Salmon decline reduces one fish prey available to kingfishers.

relationships.description: Foxes occasionally take barn owl eggs and chicks from ground-accessible nest sites.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Minor predation pressure; elevated nest boxes mitigate this risk.

relationships.description: Foxes opportunistically predate water voles along riverbanks.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Fox predation adds to cumulative pressures on water vole populations.

relationships.description: Frogs are seasonally important in fox diet, particularly during spring breeding aggregations.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Fox predation contributes to predation pressure on frogs during vulnerable breeding season.

relationships.description: Earthworm activity improves soil moisture and structure in habitats used by frogs for foraging and overwintering.
relationships.cascadeEffect: Earthworm decline degrades terrestrial habitat quality for frogs.
